opus-5.5.text:
Well, because the number of qubits, by itself, is almost meaningless. Anyone can say they have a thousand qubits, or a million qubits, but if those qubits are so noisy that you can only do a handful of operations before everything decoheres into garbage, then you don't really have a quantum computer in any useful sense. You have a very expensive random number generator.

What really matters is: can you entangle the qubits with each other reliably, over and over, for long enough to run an interesting computation? And the two-qubit gate is where the action is, because that's the operation that creates entanglement. Single-qubit gates have been very good for a long time. The two-qubit gates are the hard part, and they're typically the dominant source of error.

So the key number I look at is the two-qubit gate fidelity. For years it was stuck around 99%, which sounds great until you realize it means one error in every hundred operations, so after a few hundred gates your computation is dead. What's happened in the last few years, and why I've gotten more optimistic, is that several groups, with trapped ions, neutral atoms, and superconducting qubits, have gotten to 99.9% and in some cases beyond. That matters enormously because of the threshold theorem of quantum fault tolerance. Once your physical error rate is below a certain threshold, you can use quantum error correction to encode logical qubits that are much more reliable than the physical ones, and in principle compute for as long as you want. But you have to be comfortably below that threshold, or the overhead becomes astronomical.

So for me, the story of quantum computing right now isn't "look how many qubits we have." It's "look how close we're getting to the regime where error correction actually works." Once you're there, scaling up the qubit count becomes, in some sense, an engineering problem: very hard engineering, but not something requiring new physics. That's why, if a company press release leads with the qubit count and doesn't tell me the gate fidelities, my first reaction is skepticism.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the simple answer is that qubit count is the number that's easy to hype, and gate fidelity is the number that actually determines whether you can do anything. I could give you a million qubits tomorrow if you don't care how good they are. Every atom in this room is a qubit, in some sense. The whole question is whether you can control them and entangle them while keeping errors low enough that the computation means something.

And here's the thing people often miss: the errors aren't additive in a benign way. If your two-qubit gates each fail with probability, say, one percent, then after a few hundred gates you've basically got noise. It doesn't matter if you have fifty qubits or five thousand, you're not running a deep circuit. So the depth of what you can do is set by the fidelity, not the width.

The deeper reason I care about it is error correction. We've known since the late nineties, from the threshold theorem, that if you can get your physical gates below some error rate, you can in principle correct the errors faster than they accumulate, and then scale up arbitrarily. But that threshold is demanding, and the overhead depends enormously on how far below it you are. Being just under threshold means you might need a thousand physical qubits for one good logical qubit. Being well under it brings that down dramatically. So improvements in fidelity from ninety-nine percent to ninety-nine point nine percent are not marginal. They change the whole economics of the thing.

So when I'm trying to judge whether the field is actually progressing, I look at the two-qubit gate error rate, because that's the hard physics. Single-qubit gates have been good for a long time. It's the entangling gates, the ones where you actually have to make two systems talk to each other without letting the environment join the conversation, that are the bottleneck. That number going down is what I'd call real progress. The qubit count going up, by itself, tells me mostly about the press release.

astra-6.text:
Well, because the goal is not just to have a lot of qubits. The goal is to perform a computation with them, and that means making them interact reliably. Two-qubit gates are what let you create entanglement and do the operations that give quantum computing its power. They’re also typically much harder to get right than operations on individual qubits.

If those gates are too noisy, then as you perform more of them, the errors accumulate, and your computation becomes useless before you’ve done anything interesting. Adding more qubits doesn’t solve that problem. You could have a million qubits, but if you can’t reliably operate on them, you don’t have a useful quantum computer.

Now, quantum error correction gives us a way forward, but it requires the underlying operations to be sufficiently accurate. And improving that accuracy can dramatically reduce the overhead needed for error correction. So qubit count matters, of course, but I want to know: how good are the qubits? How reliably can you perform two-qubit gates? That tells you much more about how close you are to doing a substantial computation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether a device can perform useful or substantial computations, but does not identify outperforming a classical computer as the test.

r002.rationale: It says adding more qubits does not solve unreliable, noisy two-qubit gates, making clear that higher qubit count does not necessarily mean higher gate fidelity.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, because it’s relatively easy to have a lot of qubits if you don’t require them to do anything useful. The hard part is getting those qubits to interact in a controlled way while preserving their quantum coherence. Two-qubit gate fidelity measures how reliably you can perform those interactions, which are essential for general quantum computation.

Every gate introduces some error. If the error rate is too high, then as you perform more operations, the noise overwhelms the computation. Adding more qubits doesn’t solve that problem; it can just give you a larger noisy system.

Quantum error correction offers a way out, but it requires the underlying operations to be sufficiently accurate. And even once you’re below the relevant error threshold, improving fidelity can dramatically reduce the number of physical qubits you need to encode a reliable logical qubit.

So qubit count certainly matters, but it has to be considered together with the quality of the operations. What we ultimately care about is how large and how reliable a computation you can actually carry out.
